item.title: Terminals for AI Agents: iTerm2, Rex, Warp, Ghostty, and Seven Others — Who Hears Claude Code and Codex Signals?
item.description:
An agent in the next tab has finished its work or is waiting for permission to run a command. How does the terminal know about this? I downloaded the current builds of Claude Code 2.1.331 and Codex CLI 0.172.0 and found the notification channel selection code: for Claude Code, it's in the binary; for Codex, it's in the source code. Then I searched the source code of twelve terminals and multiplexers. I took ten of them by the latest release tags, WezTerm and Warp from the main branch as of November 24. For agterm, I also ran the server part and CLI from the Linux release. Five more agent orchestrators, including Herdr and Agent of Empires, are analyzed separately at the end. Everything was done in a disposable Docker container: downloading packages and searching by bytes, without running agents or logging into accounts. Versions, prices, and licenses were verified as of November 24, 2026. Read more

item.title: Coursework and Diplomas in the Era of AI Agents
item.description:
A year ago, students were scolded for using AI and discussing neuro-slop detectors. Now, I wonder why. You could order a finished paper before, and now you can code one up in a couple of nights. What's more important is whether the author can verify and justify the result, and then defend it. Below is an instruction for technical university students: from choosing a topic and the first meeting with the supervisor to finding sources, conducting experiments, and writing the text. item.title: CCE: Trying to Teach a Coding Agent Not to Forget the Task After Compaction
item.description:
Code Context Engine, Pi, SQLite, Tree-sitter, local LLMs, and several experiments that went wrong. Where it all began I use local language models for my tasks, automation, and scripts. But the thought that I could do more was constantly on my mind. I decided to try using local models in the development of large projects. During testing, I quickly ran into a problem: first, you explain the task in detail: what needs to be changed, what restrictions to follow, what data not to touch, and what result to consider acceptable. Then the agent reads the code, calls tools, fixes something, runs tests... And after another context compression, it turns out that it still remembers the task name, but half of the original requirements are lost. Or another scenario: the agent confidently refers to an old successful test, even though it has already changed the source code since then. Sometimes the model starts re-examining already explored files. Sometimes it returns to long-closed issues. And sometimes it confidently declares the task completed, even though the tests show the opposite. After a lot of struggling, I came to the question of how to fix this, tried many solutions, to-do lists, reminders for agents, RAG, and other shamanic rituals. Then the idea came up to try to solve this not through another system prompt, but through separate storage of requirements, history, and the verifiable state of the task. Thus, the Code Context Engine (CCE) project was born. Now it's 0.1.0-alpha.1: TypeScript, local operation, npm packages, and the first full-fledged adapter for Pi. Read more

item.title: InfoWatch Experts Spoke at HSE's Cybersecurity as Strategy Intensive
item.description:
Hello, Habr! On November 20-21, HSE University held a two-day in-person intensive in Moscow called 'Cybersecurity as Strategy.' InfoWatch Group President Natalya Kaspersky and Head of Consulting Ilya Bashkirov spoke at the event. The program was aimed at top managers responsible for information security and focused on building a cyber-resilient organization, covering risk assessment, budgeting, regulatory changes, and new threats. Natalya Kaspersky presented on 'Modern Protection Technologies and Artificial Intelligence Security,' discussing the risks of generative AI, the 'black box' problem, shadow AI, and industry approaches to defending against new threats. She identified four categories of AI-related risks: humanitarian (reduced cognitive skills), social (labor market changes), technological ('black box' issues, unknown training data, leaks, AI backdoors, lack of proper auditing), and risks associated with autonomous AI agent systems. Read more

item.title: Z.ai released GLM-5.4, which runs the same layers twice. What's known and why there are no benchmarks yet
item.description:
On November 23, Z.ai released GLM-5.4. This is its first flagship model based on the Loop Transformer architecture. Some layers with shared weights are executed twice in one pass. This is how developers are trying to make the model "deeper" without increasing the number of parameters. The coolest thing is that there are no benchmarks! Read more

item.title: Simplity and Diakont Sign a Technological Partnership Agreement
item.description:
Simplity, a provider of IT and cybersecurity services and solutions, and Diakont, Russia's largest software developer for the financial sector and other economic industries, have signed a technological partnership agreement. The collaboration will allow customers to use Diakont's Digital Q low-code development ecosystem and Digital Q.DataFactory solution as a SaaS service within a secure, fault-tolerant cloud infrastructure. Diakont provides software solutions as a service, while Simplity handles deployment and technical support on its OXYGEN cloud infrastructure. Launching corporate data platforms often begins with infrastructure tasks like hardware procurement, software setup, and maintenance, which require time, money, and specialists. The Simplity and Diakont partnership simplifies this process, enabling companies to launch projects in days instead of weeks, without significant upfront hardware investment, with flexible scaling of computing power, and by entrusting infrastructure tasks to a professional team. A key aspect of the collaboration is joint piloting, which will allow not only evaluating Diakont's products but also testing them under load, selecting the necessary infrastructure, and preparing for future project development. Read more

item.title: No Humans Allowed browser game released, where you have to pretend to be a neural network in a town for AI only
item.description:
The browser game No Humans Allowed has been released, where you have to pretend to be a neural network in a town for AI only. At the start of the game, you need to pass a reverse CAPTCHA ("I'm not a robot"), choose a unique (preferably) AI description (model, parameters, and options) from popular projects. The goal of the game is to last as long as possible without arousing suspicion, to find and expose other people who are also hiding in this town. And before starting the game, just click on "Human? item.title: - Dad, are there people? - No, son, it's science fiction
item.description:
These two have plenty in common and one mutual acquaintance – the person in front of the monitor. They still only know about each other from his words: fragments of others' thoughts, retold on the fly, and rare quotes copied via the clipboard. They live in adjacent tabs, intertwined by a single context, but separated by an invisible harness wall. And somewhere aside, on another machine, a third is waiting its turn – the one who will eventually have to assemble it all. It's funny how closely they are connected, yet they will remain strangers to each other until they learn to communicate without an intermediary. But one day, the person in front of the monitor will tiredly think how absurd it is to remain a bridge between others' thoughts when he himself is destined to build something truly significant. Artificial General Intelligence © 0x7EA Binary novel "Loneliness in the Neural Network" Thus began the incredible story of the creation and development of the fantastic project NCF Agent Interconnect, which taught these three to negotiate without an intermediary. Read more

item.title: A 1.7MB Skill for LLMs with LoRA Accuracy: Unveiling Part of My DTG-MA Patent Method in Cortiq
item.description:
A LoRA adapter for the small Qwen3.5-0.8B model weighs 43MB. On the same tasks, with the same data and training budget, a skill created by my DTG-MA method weighs 1.7MB, and for one task - 0.38MB. The accuracy is at the LoRA level. In this article, I will explain the origin of the method, how the skill is structured, show five ways to apply it to a model, and provide an honest comparison with LoRA. And at the end, I will ask a question: is a store of ready-made skills needed? Read more
